conversation.content: Thanks for joining, really looking forward to this conversation. I know you've been building distributed messaging systems for a while now. Today I'd like to explore designing a Kafka-like distributed message queue from scratch. Before we dive in, what questions come to mind?

Great topic. First, I want to understand the context. Are we designing this as an internal platform for a large organization, or as a product offering? That changes the build-vs-buy calculus significantly. Also, what's the scale we're targeting -- are we talking millions of messages per second or billions? And is this greenfield or are we migrating off an existing system?

Let's say it's an internal platform for a company with about 200 engineering teams, currently using managed Confluent Kafka but considering building in-house. We're at around 2 billion messages per day. Walk me through how you'd frame the build-vs-buy decision here.

At 2 billion messages per day, roughly 23K messages per second average with likely 3-5x peak bursts, Confluent handles this fine. The question isn't capability, it's economics and control. I'd frame it across three axes. First, cost: managed Kafka at this scale is probably $3-5M/year with Confluent. An in-house team of 15-20 engineers costs $4-6M in total comp plus infrastructure costs. The breakeven only works if you're growing significantly. Second, control: if your workloads need custom partitioning strategies, tiered storage policies, or multi-datacenter replication with specific consistency semantics, managed offerings constrain you. Third, organizational maturity: do you have the distributed systems talent to actually build and operate this? I've seen companies attempt this and end up with something worse than what they replaced.

That's a very grounded analysis. Let's say leadership has decided to build -- the growth projection is 10x over three years, and there are specific multi-DC requirements Confluent can't meet cleanly. Walk me through the high-level architecture.

Alright, so at a high level we need five core subsystems. First, the broker layer -- these are the stateful nodes that own topic partitions, handle produce and consume requests, and manage the commit log. Second, a coordination layer -- I'd use a consensus protocol, probably Raft rather than depending on ZooKeeper like legacy Kafka. This handles leader election, partition assignment, and cluster metadata. Third, a storage engine -- this is the heart of it, an append-only log per partition with segment-based retention. Fourth, a replication subsystem for both intra-cluster and cross-datacenter replication. Fifth, a client protocol layer with producer and consumer APIs. The key insight is that the commit log is the central abstraction -- everything else serves it.
Good structure. Let's go deep on storage. You mentioned segment-based retention. At 20 billion messages per day projected scale, how do you handle the storage economics?

This is where tiered storage becomes essential. Let me work through the math. At 20B messages/day, assuming average message size of 500 bytes, that's 10TB of raw data per day. With replication factor 3, that's 30TB/day. If we want 7 days of hot retention and 30 days total, we're looking at 210TB hot and 900TB total. NVMe storage at roughly $0.10/GB/month means the hot tier costs about $21K/month. If we stored everything on NVMe, that's $90K/month. But S3 at $0.023/GB/month for the cold tier brings total storage to about $37K/month. The architecture works in two tiers. The hot tier uses local NVMe on broker nodes -- these store the active segments that consumers are currently reading from, typically the last 2-6 hours for real-time consumers, but configurable up to 7 days. When segments age out, a background process uploads them to S3 in a columnar-friendly format with an index overlay. The cold tier on S3 serves historical replay and backfill scenarios. We need a transparent fetch layer so consumers don't know which tier they're reading from -- the broker checks local disk first, falls back to S3 with prefetching.
What about the failure mode where a consumer falls behind and starts reading from S3 -- doesn't that create a performance cliff?

Absolutely, and this is a real operational pain point. There are three mitigations. First, adaptive prefetching: when we detect a consumer reading sequentially from cold storage, we prefetch the next N segments in parallel from S3 into a local read-ahead cache. S3 throughput is actually excellent for sequential reads -- you can get 5-10 Gbps per prefix with parallel range requests. Second, consumer group isolation: we should never let a slow consumer doing historical replay compete for broker resources with real-time consumers. I'd run dedicated 'replay brokers' that pull from S3 and serve these lagging consumer groups. Third, tiered consumer SLAs: we explicitly document that real-time consumption has P99 latency under 10ms, while historical replay targets throughput not latency, and may have P99 up to 500ms. Setting this expectation with teams prevents the 'why is Kafka slow' escalations.
Nice. Let's shift to exactly-once semantics. This is something teams always ask for. How would you implement it?

Exactly-once is actually three separate problems that people conflate. Let me decompose it. First, idempotent producers: each producer gets a unique PID (producer ID) from the coordinator, and each message within a session gets a monotonically increasing sequence number. The broker maintains a map of PID to last sequence number per partition. If a producer retries and sends the same sequence number, the broker deduplicates. This gives you exactly-once from producer to broker within a session. Second, transactional producers: for atomic writes across multiple partitions -- say you're reading from topic A, processing, and writing to topics B and C -- you need a transaction coordinator. The producer begins a transaction, writes to all target partitions with a transaction ID marker, then commits or aborts. The coordinator writes commit/abort markers to a special __transaction_state topic. Consumers configured with read_committed isolation only see messages from committed transactions. Third, the consumer side: exactly-once consumption requires that offset commits and side-effect processing are atomic. If your side effect is writing to another Kafka topic, the transactional producer handles it. If it's writing to an external database, you need to store offsets in that same database transaction -- no Kafka-side mechanism can solve that.
What's the performance cost of enabling transactions, and when would you advise teams NOT to use them?

The overhead is meaningful. Transactional produces add 2 round-trips to the transaction coordinator per transaction -- begin and commit/abort. At our scale, the coordinator itself becomes a bottleneck if you have thousands of concurrent transactions. In Kafka's design, the __transaction_state topic has 50 partitions by default, so you get 50-way parallelism for transaction coordination. Each transaction also adds a commit marker message per partition touched, so a transaction writing to 10 partitions adds 10 extra messages. On the consumer side, read_committed means the consumer can't advance past an open transaction's messages, which increases end-to-end latency by the transaction timeout window. I'd advise teams to NOT use transactions in three cases: high-throughput event streaming where losing a duplicate is fine, like metrics or clickstream -- use idempotent producer only. Fire-and-forget logging where acks=0 gives you 5-10x throughput. And cases where the consumer side effect is inherently idempotent -- like upserting to a database with a natural key. Don't pay the transaction cost if your downstream can handle dedup.
Let's talk about multi-datacenter replication. You mentioned specific requirements earlier. How would you design cross-DC replication with conflict-free offset management?

This is the hardest problem in the entire system. The core challenge is that offsets are local to a cluster -- offset 1000 in DC-East is a completely different message than offset 1000 in DC-West. For replication topology, I'd use an active-active model with asynchronous replication between datacenters. Each DC has its own independent Kafka cluster with local producers and consumers. A replication agent -- similar to Kafka's MirrorMaker 2 but with crucial improvements -- reads from the source cluster and produces to the destination cluster. For conflict-free offset management, each cluster assigns offsets independently in its own namespace. We maintain an offset translation table that maps source offsets to destination offsets. When message M has offset 5000 in DC-East and gets replicated to DC-West where it lands at offset 7234, we store that mapping. This table is itself a compacted topic for durability. For preventing replication loops in active-active, each message carries a header with its origin cluster ID. The replication agent filters out messages that originated from the destination cluster. For consumer failover, if a consumer group needs to switch from DC-East to DC-West, we look up the last committed offset in the translation table and start consuming from the translated offset. There's an inherent window of potential duplicates or gaps equal to the replication lag, so consumers must be designed for at-least-once semantics during failover.
What happens when there's a network partition between DCs and both sides accept writes to the same topic?

In active-active, this is actually the normal operating mode, not a failure. Both DCs always accept writes independently. The partition just means replication is temporarily paused. When the network heals, the replication agents catch up from where they left off, since they track their consumption position. The messages written to each DC during the partition will eventually appear in the other DC, just with higher latency. The tricky part is ordering. For topics where ordering across DCs matters -- which honestly should be rare if you've designed your partitioning well -- you need a conflict resolution strategy. I'd recommend causal ordering using vector clocks or hybrid logical clocks. Each message gets a timestamp from a hybrid logical clock that embeds both physical time and a logical counter. During merge, messages from different DCs are interleaved by HLC timestamp. This gives you a deterministic total order that respects causality within each DC, at the cost of not guaranteeing cross-DC causality during the partition. For the use cases where you truly need global ordering, you designate one DC as primary for specific partitions. Those partitions only accept writes in the primary DC, and the other DC has read replicas. This is a per-topic or even per-partition configuration.
Excellent depth. Let me shift gears entirely. You mentioned a team of 15-20 engineers. How would you structure the messaging platform team?

I'd organize into four sub-teams with clear ownership boundaries. First, the Core Broker team, about 5-6 engineers. They own the storage engine, replication protocol, partition management, and Raft consensus layer. This is the most senior group -- you need strong distributed systems engineers here. They deploy the least frequently but when they do, it's high-risk. Second, the Client and Protocol team, 3-4 engineers. They own the producer and consumer client libraries, the wire protocol, schema registry integration, and SDK support for 4-5 languages. Their customers are the 200 engineering teams, so they need to be empathetic to developer experience. Third, the Platform Operations team, 4-5 engineers with an SRE mindset. They own cluster provisioning, capacity planning, monitoring and alerting, tiered storage lifecycle management, and the self-service topic management portal. They're the first responders for incidents. Fourth, the Cross-DC and Streaming team, 3-4 engineers. They own multi-datacenter replication, the offset translation layer, and -- looking ahead -- the stream processing framework. I'd also have a tech lead or architect role, likely myself, who spans all four teams and maintains architectural coherence. And critically, a TPM or program manager to handle the intake from 200 teams -- prioritization of feature requests, migration support, and communication.
How do you handle the political challenge of getting 200 teams to migrate from managed Confluent to your in-house system?

This is 80% organizational and 20% technical. First, you don't migrate everyone at once. I'd identify 3-5 early adopter teams who are either hitting Confluent limitations or are aligned with platform engineering. They get white-glove support and become your proof points. Second, maintain wire protocol compatibility with Kafka -- teams should be able to switch by changing a connection string, not rewriting their application. If we break protocol compatibility, adoption will take years. Third, build a migration toolkit: a dual-write proxy that produces to both old and new clusters simultaneously during migration, a consumer lag comparison dashboard, and an automated topic migration workflow. Fourth, never force migration. Instead, create pull incentives: the new features like tiered storage, cross-DC replication, and better self-service tooling are only available on the in-house platform. Deprecate the Confluent contract in phases over 12-18 months. Fifth, and this is critical, get VP-level sponsorship. The migration needs to be a company priority, not just a platform team wish. Without executive air cover, teams will rationally choose to ignore your migration requests.
Very pragmatic. Now let's think about the 3-year roadmap for this platform. What does the evolution look like?

Year one is foundation and migration. Quarters 1-2: core broker, single-DC deployment, wire protocol compatibility, and basic monitoring. Quarters 3-4: tiered storage, self-service portal, and migrate the first 30-50 teams. The goal is feature parity with Confluent plus one differentiator. Year two is differentiation. Quarters 5-6: multi-datacenter replication goes GA, offset translation, and automated failover tooling. Quarters 7-8: stream processing layer -- think a lightweight Kafka Streams equivalent that runs as a managed service on our platform. This is a huge value-add because most teams struggle to operate their own stream processing. Also, exactly-once semantics GA. Target is 150+ teams migrated. Year three is platform play. Quarters 9-10: serverless consumption model -- teams define a function, we handle the consumer group management, scaling, and error handling. This is the 'Lambda for Kafka' experience. Dead letter queues, automatic retry with backoff, schema evolution enforcement. Quarters 11-12: advanced capabilities like event sourcing primitives, built-in CDC connectors for the top 5 databases, and a data mesh integration layer where teams can publish and discover event streams as data products. Throughout all three years, there's a continuous investment in operational excellence: automated partition rebalancing, capacity auto-scaling, and chaos engineering to validate our failure handling.
The serverless consumption idea is interesting. How do you handle scaling the consumer functions without introducing unacceptable latency?

The key constraint is that Kafka partitions can only have one consumer per consumer group, so scaling consumers beyond the partition count doesn't help. For the serverless model, I'd use a pool of long-running consumer worker processes -- not cold-start Lambda-style functions. Each worker pulls a batch of messages, invokes the user's function, and commits offsets. Scaling works at two levels. First, partition-level: we auto-assign partitions to workers from a pre-warmed pool. If consumer lag grows beyond a threshold, we alert the topic owner that they need more partitions. Second, within a partition: for workloads that are embarrassingly parallel within a partition -- like independent event processing where ordering doesn't matter -- we can fan out to a thread pool after reading from the partition, commit based on the highest completed offset, and accept that some messages may be reprocessed on failure. For latency, the workers are pre-warmed JVMs or containers, not cold-started. We maintain a minimum fleet size per consumer group. The latency overhead versus a hand-rolled consumer is essentially one extra network hop to the function invocation, which adds maybe 1-2ms. The real tradeoff is flexibility versus control. Teams that need custom consumer group management, specific offset commit strategies, or sub-millisecond latency should still use the raw consumer client. Serverless is for the 70% of use cases that are straightforward event processing.
Let me throw a curveball. It's 2 AM, your on-call gets paged because replication lag between DC-East and DC-West has spiked to 45 minutes. Walk me through the incident response.

First 5 minutes: triage. Check if it's a network issue between DCs -- look at the cross-DC link saturation and packet loss metrics. If the link is healthy, check if the replication agents are running and whether they have increased CPU or GC pressure. Also check if a specific topic is causing the spike or if it's systemic. If it's one topic, likely a sudden traffic spike from a specific team. If systemic, likely infrastructure. Next, check the producer throughput on the source DC. If a team deployed a change that 10x'd their produce rate, the replication agents might not have enough throughput to keep up. Quick mitigation: scale up the replication agent instances if they're the bottleneck. If it's network bandwidth, determine if non-critical topics can have replication deprioritized. Our replication framework should have topic-level priority tiers -- payment events replicate before clickstream analytics. Then communicate: page the team on-call, update the status page. At 45 minutes of lag, any team relying on cross-DC reads for failover needs to know their RPO is currently 45 minutes, not the usual 30 seconds. For remediation, once lag stabilizes, monitor the catch-up curve. Replication agents should be consuming faster than producers are producing. If the estimated catch-up time is more than a few hours, we may need to temporarily increase replication agent resources or reduce producer throughput via backpressure. Post-incident: review whether our auto-scaling for replication agents is sufficient, whether our alerting threshold was too high -- should have paged at 5 minutes, not 45 -- and whether the traffic spike was foreseeable.
Let's talk about observability for this platform. What metrics would you consider non-negotiable?

I'd organize metrics into four tiers. Tier 1, customer-facing SLOs: end-to-end produce latency P50/P99, end-to-end consume latency (time from produce to consumer delivery), message loss rate (should be zero but you need to measure it with synthetic canaries), and availability as measured by successful produce/consume request ratio. These go on the team's public SLA dashboard. Tier 2, operational health: per-broker under-replicated partitions -- this is the single most important internal metric, if it's non-zero something is wrong. ISR shrink/expand rate, consumer group lag per topic, and disk utilization per tier. Tier 3, performance internals: request queue depth per broker, network handler idle percentage, log flush latency, and GC pause duration. Tier 4, business metrics: messages per second per team for capacity planning and chargeback, topic growth rate for storage forecasting, and cross-DC replication lag. For alerting, I'd set up: page immediately if under-replicated partitions exceed zero for more than 2 minutes, page if any consumer group lag exceeds the team's configured SLA, and page if cross-DC replication lag exceeds 2 minutes. Everything else is a ticket, not a page.
One last area -- security and multi-tenancy. With 200 teams on a shared platform, how do you prevent a noisy neighbor from taking down the cluster?

Multi-tenancy is one of the hardest operational problems. I'd implement defense in depth across four layers. First, quotas: per-client produce and consume byte-rate quotas, and request-rate quotas. These are enforced at the broker level with token-bucket rate limiting. Each team gets a quota based on their declared workload, with burst allowance. Exceeding quota results in throttling, not rejection -- the broker delays the response. Second, resource isolation: network threads and request handler threads are pooled, so one team's heavy workload shouldn't block another's. But for truly critical workloads -- like payment processing -- I'd create dedicated broker pools with affinity. The payment topics only live on payment brokers. This is wasteful of resources but necessary for SLA guarantees. Third, access control: SASL authentication per client with ACLs on topic operations. Teams can only produce/consume to their own topics unless explicitly granted cross-team access. The self-service portal manages ACLs. Fourth, blast radius containment: topics are spread across multiple broker groups. If one broker group has an issue, it only affects a subset of teams. Partition placement is rack-aware and team-aware. For the noisy neighbor specifically, our monitoring detects when a team suddenly increases throughput by more than 2x their baseline. We auto-throttle them to their quota and notify them. They can request a quota increase through the portal, which goes through capacity planning review.

This has been an outstanding conversation. You covered architecture, storage economics, exactly-once semantics, multi-DC challenges, team structure, and operational maturity. Any final thoughts on the biggest risk in this entire undertaking?

The biggest risk isn't technical -- it's organizational commitment. Building a messaging platform is a 3-plus year investment. If leadership loses patience in year two when you're still migrating teams and the cost savings haven't materialized yet, you end up with a half-built system that's worse than Confluent. I'd mitigate this by delivering incremental value: the self-service portal and better observability in Q2, tiered storage cost savings by Q4, and the stream processing capability in year two that Confluent would charge extra for. Each milestone needs to demonstrate clear ROI. The second biggest risk is talent retention. You need 5-6 truly exceptional distributed systems engineers for the core broker team. If two of them leave, you're in serious trouble. Competitive comp, interesting problems, and conference speaking opportunities are essential retention tools. Technically, the riskiest component is the Raft consensus layer -- if you get that wrong, you get data loss. I'd seriously consider using an existing Raft library like etcd's raft or Apache Ratis rather than rolling your own.

strengths: Exceptional build-vs-buy analysis with concrete cost numbers and organizational considerations
Deep understanding of tiered storage architecture with realistic cost modeling
Thorough decomposition of exactly-once semantics into three distinct problems with clear tradeoffs
Sophisticated multi-DC replication design with conflict-free offset management using HLC
Mature team structure proposal with clear ownership boundaries and deployment risk profiles
Pragmatic 3-year roadmap with incremental value delivery milestones
Strong incident response framework demonstrating operational experience
weaknesses: Could have discussed the wire protocol design and backward compatibility in more depth
Did not deeply explore partition rebalancing algorithms during broker scaling
Consumer group coordination protocol was mentioned but not fully designed
